newsitem.title: UK: Slim winter fuel stocks reignite oil price rally.
newsitem.headline: Slim winter fuel stocks reignite oil price rally.

text.p: A rally in world oil prices was reignited on Wednesday by further signs that big western consumers have not built up enough heating fuel stocks ahead of winter in the northern hemisphere.
November futures for benchmark Brent Blend crude oil in London jumped 24 cents to $23.31 per barrel at 1515 GMT, extending a rally which began in June and has already pushed prices up by a third.

Inventories of heating oil in the United States, the world's biggest energy user, were 29 percent below last year, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, and were also below normal in Europe, traders said.

Heating oil prices on the London futures market have spiralled even more than crude, by 50 percent in the past three months to a five-year high of $242.00 per tonne on Wednesday, and dealers saw no end in sight for the rally.
"I do not see why these prices should come down," said Benoit Renie, a trader at French oil company Total.
"We have got very low stocks and end-users don't want to buy because of the high prices. But they have delayed their purchases and one day they will have to buy," he said.
In Europe, the highest priced heating oil market in the world, the stock problem was exacerbated by a change to low-pollution diesel which took place on October 1, he added.

"The change to low sulphur diesel has created logistical constraints in refineries, pipelines and marketing, and that means we have even lower stocks than we would do otherwise," Renie said. "All this means we have very high prices and they could go higher."
The high price of heating oil, in particular, has become a political issue in the United States ahead of presidential elections on November 5.
Oil is the primary fuel for domestic heating in the U.S. northeast, and the average consumer there could face an extra $200 in bills this winter, U.S. economists estimated recently.
U.S. Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary said on Tuesday she was investigating ways of preventing a price spike.
She suggested Venezuela, the biggest oil producer in South America, might be able to increase shipments, but traders said only higher U.S. prices would attract cargoes into American ports.
"The way the market works, wherever it can be sold at the highest price, that's where it will go," said Ron Planting, a statistician at the American Petroleum Institute.
